events.text: Objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.; Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.; Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.; 2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.; 3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.; 4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments..

Simonelli can capture value by positioning its premium machines as essential tools for the home barista lifestyle. Who benefits: Home baristas and coffee enthusiasts who value quality and convenience in a compact form.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers are increasingly viewing coffee as a lifestyle experience and are willing to invest in equipment that allows them to create professional-quality espresso at home.. How value is captured: Simonelli can charge premium prices for its machines and capture margin through direct-to-consumer sales and brand positioning as a premium home barista brand.. T2: Consumers are adopting home espresso machines as a convenience and time-saving solution, particularly in urban environments where access to coffee shops is limited. Why behaviour changes: Consumers are prioritizing convenience and efficiency in their daily routines, leading them to choose equipment that minimizes preparation time and space requirements.. How value is captured: Simonelli can sell compact machines at a premium price, leveraging its reputation for quality and design to attract consumers who value convenience over bulkiness.. T1: Homeowners and renters will purchase consumer-grade laundry machines at higher price points because they view them as a convenience and status upgrade, not just a functional appliance. Who benefits: Homeowners, renters, and small landlords seeking convenience and modern aesthetics.. Why behaviour changes: Growing consumer demand for stylish, integrated home appliances and the convenience of self-service laundry reduce perceived utility of basic, utility-style appliances.. How value is captured: Electrolux can charge premium prices for design, smart features, and brand positioning, and potentially license its technology to brands for consumer machines.. Assumptions: Consumers perceive self-service laundry as a modern amenity.; Price sensitivity for home buyers is lower than for professional buyers.; Electrolux's design credibility can be leveraged in consumer markets.. Predictions: Willingness-to-pay studies show consumers will pay at least 20% more for a designer self-service unit than a standard machine.; Consumer surveys indicate a desire for aesthetic integration with home decor.; Pilot sales show higher conversion rates for premium-priced units in pilot markets..

T2: Small businesses and rental properties will adopt consumer-grade laundry machines because they need reliable, low-cost solutions for guest laundry and staff facilities, and existing professional machines are too expensive or difficult to service. Who benefits: Small hotels, gyms, campsites, marinas, and rental property owners with limited budgets.. Why behaviour changes: High turnover of guest laundry and staff facilities makes it cheaper to replace machines than to upgrade, and consumers prefer machines that are easy to maintain and repair.. How value is captured: Electrolux can sell lower-priced, easier-to-service units through retail and wholesale channels, and potentially offer service contracts to reduce downtime.. Assumptions: Small businesses have limited capital for new equipment.; Current professional machines are difficult to repair or replace.; Consumers prioritize ease of maintenance over brand prestige.. Predictions: Small business surveys show higher purchase intent for machines priced under $2,000 compared to professional-grade units.; Pilot sales in rental properties show higher adoption rates for machines with modular designs.; Customer satisfaction surveys highlight ease of repair as a key purchase driver..

Test "Premium vs. Value Messaging Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners/renters and 250 small business owners/rental property managers, recruited via panel to match demographics.. Measure: Average WTP (in euros) for a self-service laundry unit described with either premium design features (status upgrade) or cost-ease-of-maintain features (small business). Secondary measure: stated purchase intent (1‑10).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher WTP for premium-priced units (e.g., €1,500‑€2,000) than small businesses will show higher WTP for value-priced units (e.g., €1,000‑€1,500).; T2: Small businesses will show higher WTP for value-priced units (e.g., €1,000‑€1,500) than homeowners will show higher WTP for premium-priced units.. Decision rule: If homeowners’ average WTP for premium units exceeds small businesses’ average WTP for value units by at least €500, proceed to develop a differentiated premium consumer proposition. If small businesses’ average WTP for value units exceeds homeowners’ average WTP for premium units by at least €500, develop a value‑focused small‑business proposition. If both thresholds are met, pursue both propositions; otherwise, no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not yet commit to a full consumer proposition. Public evidence shows residential demand for commercial-quality home machines (Alliance Laundry Holdings) and a self-service format capability (Electrolux), but no direct proof of premium pricing or status motivation. Run the proposed premium‑vs‑value messaging pilot to test willingness to pay before investing. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer motivation, pricing, or small business demand. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not yet commit to a full consumer proposition. Public evidence shows residential demand for commercial-quality home machines (Alliance Laundry Holdings) and a self-service format capability (Electrolux), but no direct proof of premium pricing or status motivation. Run the proposed premium-vs-value messaging pilot to test willingness to pay before investing. Target customer: Homeowners and renters seeking convenience and modern aesthetics, and small businesses with limited budgets for guest laundry and staff facilities.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that combines professional-grade performance with design, smart features, and ease of use, enabling homeowners to run their own laundry and small businesses to provide reliable, low-cost guest laundry.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 8‑week, €18,000 premium-vs-value messaging pilot with 500 respondents to measure willingness to pay for premium‑priced units versus value‑priced units.. Uncertainty: The size of the premium price premium homeowners will pay and whether small businesses will adopt at lower price points remain uncertain. Evidence of actual purchase intent and market share is lacking.. Would change if: If the pilot shows homeowners’ average willingness to pay for premium units exceeds small businesses’ average willingness to pay for value units by at least €500, we would proceed to develop a differentiated premium consumer proposition.; If small businesses show higher willingness to pay for value units, we would develop a value‑focused small‑business proposition.; If neither threshold is met, we would maintain the current professional‑only focus.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Premium vs. Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (focus on health benefits, taste, and purity) or Sustainability Condition (focus on reducing plastic waste and environmental impact). Both conditions present a differentiated home water purifier at the same price point. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark and Turkey, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income levels.. Measure: Purchase intent score in the Premium Condition versus the Sustainability Condition, and maximum price willingness to pay.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Sustainability Condition.; T2: Sustainability Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Premium Condition.. Decision rule: If Premium Condition purchase intent exceeds Sustainability Condition by at least 10 points (e.g., Premium ≥ 65, Sustainability ≤ 55) AND the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a differentiated premium consumer proposition. If Sustainability Condition exceeds Premium Condition by at least 10 points AND the difference is statistically significant, proceed with a sustainability‑focused proposition. If neither condition meets the threshold, do not expand the consumer proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Consumer vs Business Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners/renters and 250 small business owners (hotels, gyms, campsites). Recruit via social media and industry forums.. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a compact self-service machine and intent to purchase based on messaging (convenience vs cost efficiency).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher WTP and purchase intent when messaging emphasizes convenience and reduced wait times.; T2: Small businesses will show higher WTP and purchase intent when messaging emphasizes cost savings and labor reduction.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the convenience message exceeds the average WTP for the cost-efficiency message by at least 10% among homeowners, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience. If the cost-efficiency message outperforms by at least 10% among small businesses, develop a consumer proposition focused on cost savings. If both thresholds are met, pursue both propositions.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Smart vs Premium Combi-Steamer Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 home cooks recruited via a panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and WTP (dollar amount).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of respondents will indicate purchase intent for the subscription-based smart model, and the average WTP will be at least €150 (monthly subscription).; T2: At least 35% of respondents will indicate purchase intent for the premium, high-performance model, and the average WTP will be at least €200 (premium price).. Decision rule: If the smart model meets both thresholds (purchase intent ≥30% and WTP ≥€150), proceed to develop a subscription-based home-cook proposition. If the premium model meets both thresholds, proceed to develop a premium, high-performance home-cook proposition. If neither meets thresholds, maintain current B2B focus.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated subscription-based smart combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi-steamer technology and B2B reputation. The test should validate purchase intent and willingness to pay for a subscription model before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address home cooks' willingness to pay a subscription fee or their preference for smart features. Therefore it bears on no theory and changes nothing. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated subscription-based smart combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi-steamer technology and B2B reputation. Target customer: Home cooks who value convenience, automation, and recurring revenue, particularly those who already use smart home devices and are willing to pay a monthly subscription.. Value proposition: A smart, subscription-based combi-steamer that automates cooking, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing value, reducing upfront cost and offering a recurring revenue stream.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 12‑week online survey test with 500 home cooks to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the subscription model. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with development.. Uncertainty: The willingness of home cooks to pay a monthly subscription fee for a smart combi-steamer is uncertain. Additionally, the competitive landscape and RATIONAL’s ability to adapt its technology to a residential subscription model are unknown.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 30% or average willingness to pay below €150, the recommendation would shift to maintain the current B2B focus.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for premium, high‑performance models, the recommendation could shift to develop a premium proposition instead.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Smart vs Premium vs Health Messaging Test" between T1; T2; T3. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: Smart Group (smart features and subscription messaging), Premium Group (design and brand prestige messaging), Health Group (health and low-impact messaging). Each group sees a product description of a differentiated combi-steamer and is asked to indicate willingness to pay a fixed price (e.g., €1,200) and to choose a purchase channel (online, retail).. Sample: 300 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three groups (100 per group).. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. 2) Purchase intent (binary: would buy). 3) Channel preference (online vs retail).. Predictions: T1: Smart Group will show the highest WTP and purchase intent among home cooks, while Premium and Health Groups will show lower WTP and purchase intent.; T2: Premium Group will show the highest WTP and purchase intent, while Smart and Health Groups will show lower WTP and purchase intent.; T3: Health Group will show the highest WTP and purchase intent, while Smart and Premium Groups will show lower WTP and purchase intent.. Decision rule: If the Smart Group's average WTP is at least 20% higher than the Premium Group's and at least 15% higher than the Health Group's, we conclude that smart features drive adoption and recommend developing a differentiated home-cook proposition with smart and subscription capabilities. Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions (premium messaging or sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2 to 7) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium messaging will yield a higher average purchase intent score than sustainability messaging.; T2: Sustainability messaging will yield a higher average purchase intent score than premium messaging.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for premium messaging is at least 1.5 points higher than for sustainability messaging, conclude that premium positioning drives higher demand and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on taste and purity. If sustainability messaging is higher, recommend a sustainability‑focused proposition. If the difference is below 1.5 points, indicate insufficient evidence to recommend a differentiated proposition and suggest further market research.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Who benefits: Health-conscious home cooks willing to pay a premium for convenience and health advantages.. Why behaviour changes: If RATIONAL frames the product as a modern, stylish appliance that delivers faster, healthier meals, they will shift from generic appliances to a premium offering.. How value is captured: Higher price points and repeat purchases from a niche segment of affluent home cooks.. Assumptions: Home cooks perceive steam-cooking as a benefit.; There is a segment willing to pay a premium for design and convenience.; Marketing can differentiate RATIONAL's technology from competitors.. Predictions: A survey of home cooks would show at least 30% would consider purchasing a premium combi-steamer at a price 20% above standard models.; Sales would be concentrated among demographics with higher disposable income and interest in culinary gadgets..

T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer primarily because of convenience and time savings, not premium design or health benefits, because they already use multiple appliances and seek solutions that reduce cooking time. Why behaviour changes: If RATIONAL offers a compact, single-appliance solution that cooks multiple dishes simultaneously, home cooks will switch from a collection of separate appliances to a streamlined system.. How value is captured: Higher volume sales through a single product and repeat purchases due to convenience.. Assumptions: Home cooks have limited cooking time and prefer one appliance for multiple tasks.; Time savings are a primary purchase driver for home cooks.; RATIONAL can demonstrate measurable time savings in product testing.. case.question: Should Aquaporin A/S develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing water-membrane offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..

Test "Premium vs. Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants view two product concepts (standard water purifier and a differentiated version) and indicate which they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay. Messaging is randomized: premium health messaging (taste, purity) vs. sustainability messaging (plastic waste reduction).. Sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect a broad European market.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and maximum willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each concept.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher average WTP for the premium health messaging version compared to the sustainability messaging version.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher average WTP for the sustainability messaging version compared to the premium health messaging version.. Decision rule: If the premium health messaging version achieves at least 15% higher purchase intent and at least 10% higher average WTP than the sustainability messaging version, proceed with a differentiated premium health proposition. If the opposite difference holds, proceed with a differentiated sustainability proposition. If both differences are within 5 percentage points, conduct a. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a premium, health-focused water purifier, leveraging Aquaporin's existing user-friendly design and brand reputation. Begin with a limited launch in a specific segment (e.g., health-conscious households) to test demand before broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test (SYN-AQP-UPDATE) does not address consumer perception of taste, purity, or willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated product. It tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under a conditional supply assumption, which is unrelated to membrane efficacy, long-term filter use, or market size. Therefore, the evidence does not support or contradict T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-AQP-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a premium, health-focused water purifier, leveraging Aquaporin's existing user-friendly design and brand reputation. Begin with a limited launch in a specific segment (e.g., health-conscious households) to test demand before broader rollout. Target customer: Health-conscious consumers who prioritize higher purity and better taste in drinking water and are willing to pay a premium for a premium positioning.. Value proposition: A premium-priced water purifier that emphasizes superior taste, purity, and ease of use, offering a differentiated experience compared to standard models.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Premium vs. Sustainability Messaging Test (300 participants, 6 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent and willingness-to-pay differences between premium health and sustainability messaging.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to company claims and a single simulated test; no independent consumer survey data exists. The financial and market constraints of Aquaporin are also unknown from public sources.. Would change if: If the test shows the sustainability messaging version achieving at least 15% higher purchase intent and 10% higher average WTP than the premium health messaging version, we would shift focus to a sustainability proposition.; If the premium health messaging version fails to meet the threshold, we would reconsider the premium positioning and explore alternative value propositions.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Each participant views two machine concepts: (1) a high-end performance machine marketed for social interaction (e.g., a premium machine with a barista-style interface and a social hub feature). (2) a low-end convenience machine marketed for easy, consistent coffee preparation (e.g., a compact machine with automatic grinding and a built-in grinder). Participants are asked to rank the two machines on a 1-7 scale and to indicate their maximum willingness to pay (WTP) for each concept. Sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) recruited from an online panel of self-identified home baristas and coffee enthusiasts. The sample is balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and average ranking of social interaction versus convenience as the primary purchase driver for each machine concept.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. T1: Consumers will adopt self-service laundry solutions if they perceive higher convenience and lower wait times, because busy households value time savings. How value is captured: Electrolux can charge a premium for self-service units and sell additional consumables and accessories, capturing value through higher unit prices and recurring revenue.. Predictions: In a test market, households will choose a self-service unit over a traditional machine when convenience is emphasized.; Willingness to pay for a self-service unit will be at least 20% above the price of a comparable machine.; Adoption rates among households with limited time will be higher than among households with more time..

T2: Consumers will adopt self-service laundry solutions if they perceive higher cost savings and lower long-term ownership costs, because they seek to reduce recurring service and maintenance expenses. Test "Self-service vs machine choice test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: convenience condition (emphasizes time savings and self-service ease) or cost condition (emphasizes lower long-term ownership costs). They view a product description of a self-service unit and a comparable machine, and indicate which they would choose and the maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions (200 per condition).. Measure: Primary measure: choice of self-service unit vs machine. Secondary measure: maximum price willingness to pay for the chosen option.. Predictions: T1: In the convenience condition, participants will choose the self-service unit at a rate at least 15% higher than in the cost condition.; T2: In the cost condition, participants will choose the self-service unit at a rate at least 15% higher than in the convenience condition.. Decision rule: If the difference in choice rates between the two conditions is at least 15 percentage points, we conclude that the corresponding theory is supported. If the difference is less than 15 points, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported. If the difference is inconclusive, we recommend further testing.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Subscription vs Premium Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Run a targeted online pilot with two parallel A/B test groups of 200 home cooks (recruited via cooking and lifestyle platforms). Sample: 400 home cooks (200 per group) recruited from cooking and lifestyle communities.. Measure: 1) Conversion rate: percentage of participants who place a purchase order within 4 weeks. 2) Average transaction value: total amount spent per participant. 3) Post-purchase survey: self-reported willingness to pay a recurring subscription fee and perceived cooking outcome improvement.. Predictions: T1: Group A will achieve at least 10% conversion rate and an average transaction value of €1,200, while Group B will achieve less than 8% conversion rate and an average transaction value below €1,000.; T2: Group B will achieve at least 15% conversion rate and an average transaction value of €1,200, while Group A will achieve less than 10% conversion rate and an average transaction value below €1,000.. Decision rule: If Group A conversion rate ≥ 10% and its average transaction value ≥ €1,200, proceed with the subscription-based home cook proposition. If Group B conversion rate ≥ 15% and its average transaction value ≥ €1,200, proceed with the premium-priced home cook proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into either segment and maintain current focus on professional kitchens.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a full-scale home cook expansion yet. Conduct the proposed subscription vs premium pilot to test demand for a subscription-based combi-steamer. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium taste and purity messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2 to 7) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will yield a mean purchase intent score ≥ 5.5, while Sustainability Condition will yield a mean score ≤ 4.5.; T2: Sustainability Condition will yield a mean purchase intent score ≥ 5.5, while Premium Condition will yield a mean score ≤ 4.5.. Decision rule: If Premium Condition mean ≥ 5.5 and Sustainability Condition mean ≤ 4.5, conclude T1 is supported. If Sustainability Condition mean ≥ 5.5 and Premium Condition mean ≤ 4.5, conclude T2 is supported. If both conditions meet their respective thresholds, both theories are supported. Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested) and to state the top reason for choosing the product.. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark and Turkey, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium taste and purity messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability and plastic waste reduction messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested) and top reason for choosing the product.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and sustainability as top reason in Premium Condition compared to Sustainability Condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and taste and purity as top reason in Sustainability Condition compared to Premium Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score in the Premium Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than in the Sustainability Condition, and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a premium‑priced differentiated proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and consider other options.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Subscription vs Premium Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a subscription-based smart combi-steamer description emphasizing automation and recurring revenue; Group B sees a premium, professional‑grade combi-steamer description emphasizing durability and performance. Both groups are shown a product description and a willingness‑to‑pay price point (proposed at €1,500). Participants indicate intent to purchase and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and maximum willingness‑to‑pay (in euros).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B (at least 30% intent and €1,200+ willingness to pay).; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A (at least 30% intent and €1,200+ willingness to pay).. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its willingness to pay is at least €1,200, proceed with the subscription‑based smart combi-steamer development. If Group B’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its willingness to pay is at least €1,200, proceed with the premium‑priced professional‑grade combi-steamer development. If neither condition is met, do not expand into either segment and maintain current B2B focus.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Consumer vs Business Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and purchase intent questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners and 250 small businesses/commercial users recruited via targeted digital ads.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (percentage premium over professional-grade price).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than small businesses.; T2: Small businesses will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than homeowners.. Decision rule: If homeowners' purchase intent exceeds small businesses' by at least 10 percentage points and both groups' willingness to pay a premium is at least 10% above professional-grade price, conclude T1 is supported. If small businesses' intent exceeds homeowners' by at least 10 percentage points and both groups' premium is at least 10%, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the 10-point threshold, conclude neither theory is strongly supported.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.; Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.; Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).; 2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.; 4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).; 5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition..

T1: Homeowners and renters increasingly view laundry as a convenience service, leading to demand for self‑service options that reduce wait times and improve convenience. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters who lack on‑site laundry facilities and prefer quick, self‑serviced cleaning.. Why behaviour changes: Convenience and time‑saving become primary purchase drivers; self‑service removes the need to schedule a machine or wait for a person to clean.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by offering compact, self‑service machines sold directly to consumers through retail or online channels, leveraging its professional‑grade reliability to command premium pricing.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for self‑service convenience over traditional laundromats.; Regulatory and safety standards for consumer‑grade machines are met without compromising professional performance.; Retail distribution channels can effectively reach and serve individual buyers.. Predictions: In a test market, self‑service machines will achieve higher adoption rates among renters and homeowners compared to traditional laundromats.; Surveyed consumers will report convenience as the top reason for choosing a self‑service machine.; Willingness to pay will be at least 20% above the price of a comparable professional model..

T2: Small businesses and hospitality operators increasingly adopt self‑service laundry to reduce labor costs and improve operational efficiency, creating demand for compact, reliable machines that fit limited spaces. Who benefits: Small hotels, gyms, marina staff, and other small‑business operators with limited space and high turnover of laundry tasks.. Why behaviour changes: Cost savings and efficiency gains outweigh the upfront investment; self‑service eliminates the need for staff to monitor and maintain machines.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by offering compact, professional‑grade machines sold through wholesale channels to small‑business customers, leveraging its reputation for reliability and serviceability.. Assumptions: Small businesses are willing to invest in self‑service laundry to reduce labor costs.; The machines meet the performance and durability standards expected by these customers.; Wholesale distribution can effectively reach and serve small‑business operators.. Predictions: In a test market, small‑business customers will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay compared to homeowners.; Surveyed small‑business owners will cite cost savings and space efficiency as primary reasons for choosing a self‑service machine.; Adoption rates among small‑business operators will be at least 15% higher than among homeowners..

Test "Segmented Messaging Test for Self-Service Laundry" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three message conditions: (1) Homeowner convenience (self-service convenience, time savings, and premium pricing); (2) Small business efficiency (labor cost savings, space efficiency, and compact design); (3) Control (neutral message). After viewing the assigned message, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 adults (250 homeowners/renters and 250 small‑business owners) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each segment.. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than small‑business owners, and both segments will be driven primarily by convenience messaging.; T2: Small‑business owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than homeowners, and both segments will be driven primarily by efficiency messaging.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for homeowners is at least 10 points higher than for small‑business owners, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), proceed with a differentiated homeowner proposition. If the difference is less than 10 points or not statistically significant, proceed with a small‑business proposition. If both segments show similar intent differences, no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Would change if: If the test shows small‑business owners exceeding homeowners in purchase intent and willingness to pay, we would shift focus to a small‑business proposition.; If residential demand proves weak or no premium pricing is observed, we would reconsider expansion or explore alternative routes to market.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..

Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. T1: Home consumers increasingly adopt self-service laundry for convenience and cost savings, creating demand for compact, reliable consumer-grade machines that fit small spaces. Who benefits: Individual renters, small businesses, and apartment-dwelling households seeking affordable, easy-to-use laundry solutions.. Who benefits: Small hotels, gyms, marina staff, and other small businesses with limited laundry space.. Why behaviour changes: Labor shortages and rising wage costs make automated self-service solutions financially attractive, and the need to serve guests or members quickly drives adoption.. Test "Segmented Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three message groups: (1) Home self-service convenience (emphasizing compact size, energy savings, and easy use for renters and small businesses); (2) Small business operational efficiency (emphasizing labor cost savings, quick turnout, and space efficiency for hotels, gyms, and marinas); (3) Control group (no specific messaging). Participants indicate likelihood to purchase a compact professional machine at a premium price (15-20% above standard professional machines).. Sample: 500 U.S. adults (200 per segment) recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of target segments.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of respondents indicating "very likely" to purchase) for each message group.. Predictions: T1: Home self-service group will show the highest purchase intent (>=35%).; T2: Small business group will show the highest purchase intent (>=35%).. Decision rule: If the home self-service group exceeds the small business group by >=5 percentage points, recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition targeting residential self-service. If the small business group exceeds the home self-service group by >=5 percentage points, recommend a small business-focused consumer proposition. If neither segment exceeds the other by >=5 points, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows residential demand for commercial-quality home machines exists but does not demonstrate actual purchase intent or willingness to pay a premium. A proposed segmented messaging test is needed to validate demand before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer self-service demand, home laundry market growth, or small business labor cost savings. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows residential demand for commercial-quality home machines exists but does not demonstrate actual purchase intent or willingness to pay a premium. A proposed segmented messaging test is needed to validate demand before committing resources. Target customer: Residential consumers (e.g., renters, small apartment-dwelling households) seeking affordable, easy-to-use self-service laundry solutions.. Value proposition: Compact, professional-grade home machines that combine reliability, energy efficiency, and space-saving design, sold directly to consumers through retail and wholesale channels.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed segmented messaging test (500 U.S. adults, 8 weeks, €18,000) to compare purchase intent for home self-service vs. small business messaging.. Uncertainty: Actual purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium for compact consumer machines are unknown; the test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the home self-service group shows >=5 percentage points higher purchase intent than the small business group, we would recommend a differentiated residential proposition.; If neither segment exceeds the other by >=5 points, we would recommend no expansion.; If the test shows low overall intent or no premium willingness to pay, we would reconsider the investment.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners/renters and 250 small businesses (gyms, marinas, campsites). Recruit via panels to ensure diversity in age, income, and geographic location.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the self-service machine among homeowners exceeds the average WTP for the compact model by at least 10 percentage points, conclude T1 is supported. If the average WTP for the compact model among small businesses exceeds the average WTP for the self-service machine by at least 10 percentage points, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the 10-point threshold, neither theory is supported.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.; Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.; Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).; 2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.; 4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).; 5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition..

Test "Consumer vs Business Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a consumer‑operated unit (home use) and a business‑oriented unit (small business use). Participants are randomly assigned to view either the consumer or business description. They are then asked: “Would you purchase this unit?” (binary) and “What is your maximum price you would pay?” (willingness to pay).. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 homeowners (recruited via home‑laundry forums) and 150 small‑business owners (recruited via trade associations). Stratify by region to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (percentage of respondents offering a price).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than small‑business owners, indicating demand for convenience.; T2: Small‑business owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than homeowners, indicating demand for cost‑efficiency.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for the consumer unit exceeds that for the business unit by at least 10 percentage points among homeowners, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If purchase intent for the business unit exceeds that for the consumer unit by at least 10 percentage points among small‑business owners, develop a differentiated B2B proposition. If neither difference is significant, do not expand into consumer markets.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners, leveraging Electron‑x’s professional‑grade reputation and existing consumer‑operated solutions. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) tests the incremental effect of durability-and-repairability versus performance-and-price descriptions among household buyers, not actual purchase behavior. It does not address T1, which predicts homeowners will adopt self-service solutions due to convenience and cost savings. Therefore T1 remains unchanged. New claim: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions because they seek convenience, cost savings, and the ability to manage their own laundry, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners, leveraging Electron‑x’s professional‑grade reputation and existing consumer‑operated solutions. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners in multi‑family buildings, student housing, and similar residential settings who seek convenience, cost savings, and direct control over laundry timing.. Value proposition: A consumer‑operated laundry unit that combines professional‑grade reliability, easy self‑service operation, and optional premium features (e.g., smart connectivity, extended warranty) to deliver convenience and peace of mind.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Business Purchase Intent Test (300 respondents, 8 weeks, €18,000) to validate demand. If purchase intent for the consumer unit exceeds that for the business unit by at least 10 percentage points among homeowners. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay premium and the size of the homeowner market remain uncertain. Evidence of strong consumer demand is limited to the company‑assertion that consumer‑operated setups exist, and no source shows homeowners will pay. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the consumer unit is no higher than 10 percentage points than for the business unit, indicating weak demand, the recommendation would shift toward no expansion or a different route to market.; If new evidence shows homeowners are unwilling to pay a premium for self‑service units, the case for a differentiated consumer proposition would weaken.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium taste and purity messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Sustainability Condition.; T2: Sustainability Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Premium Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Premium Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Sustainability Condition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on premium taste and purity. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and consider other alternatives.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Who benefits: Home cooks gain time and reduced effort; RATIONAL benefits from recurring subscription revenue and premium pricing.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Convenience vs. Performance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from home cooks who have used traditional cooking appliances. They are shown two identical combi-steamers (same features, price, and brand) with different descriptions: one emphasizing convenience and time-saving (e.g., 'Replace multiple appliances with one device, save hours in the kitchen.'), and one emphasizing gourmet performance and professional-quality results (e.g., 'Achieve even cooking and precise temperature control like a professional chef.'). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 home cooks (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel to ensure diversity in age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the convenience-focused condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the performance-focused condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the convenience condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for the performance condition, proceed with a differentiated home-cook proposition emphasizing convenience. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, stay focused on professional kitchens. If both conditions show similar intent, conduct a follow-up survey to test price sensitivity.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of health‑conscious and environmentally conscious consumers. Each participant views a product description of a differentiated Aquaporin water purifier (same specs, price, and brand positioning). Half see a premium‑focused message emphasizing taste, purity, and health benefits; the other half see a sustainability‑focused message emphasizing reduced plastic waste and environmental impact. Participants are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) from a panel of health‑conscious and environmentally conscious consumers in Denmark and Germany.. Measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willingness to pay for the differentiated purifier.. Predictions: T1: Premium‑focused condition will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than sustainability‑focused condition.; T2: Sustainability‑focused condition will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than premium‑focused condition.. Decision rule: If the premium‑focused condition's average purchase intent exceeds the sustainability‑focused condition's average by at least 5 points (e.g., premium ≥ 6.5 vs sustainability ≥ 5.5) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a premium‑focused differentiated proposition. Otherwise, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. Test "Smart vs Premium Subscription Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Smart Group (smart, subscription-based combi-steamer) or Premium Group (premium, high-performance combi-steamer). Both groups see the same product description and price. Smart Group also receives a recurring subscription offer with a 12-week trial. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced across both groups (250 per group).. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willingness to pay for each group.. Predictions: T1: Smart Group will have higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a subscription than Premium Group.; T2: Premium Group will have higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Smart Group.. Decision rule: If Smart Group purchase intent >= 30% and Premium Group purchase intent < 20%, recommend developing a differentiated home-cook proposition (T1). If Premium Group purchase intent >= 30% and Smart Group purchase intent < 20%, recommend a premium, high-performance proposition (T2). If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition built on the existing combi-steamer technology, leveraging the subscription model to capture recurring revenue and convenience-driven demand. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cooks' willingness to pay for a subscription-based combi-steamer or the demand for a subscription model. It tests coordination friction, not subscription demand, so it does not affect T1. New claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.. Evidence: SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition built on the existing combi-steamer technology, leveraging a subscription model to capture recurring revenue and convenience-driven demand. Target customer: Home cooks who value convenience, time-saving, and recurring revenue, particularly those who already use traditional cooking appliances.. Value proposition: A smart, subscription-based combi-steamer that automates cooking, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing value, offering a lower upfront cost and continuous service compared to a premium, high-performance appliance.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Smart vs Premium Subscription Test (500 home cooks, 12 weeks, €20,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the subscription-based model versus a premium, high-performance model.. Uncertainty: The test will determine whether home cooks are willing to pay a recurring subscription fee and whether the subscription model will generate sufficient demand to justify development. The test does not address premium pricing or the size of. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the subscription-based model below 30% or willingness to pay below 20% of the device's price, the recommendation would shift to a premium, high-performance proposition (T2).; If additional evidence shows strong demand for premium features or that home cooks are unwilling to pay recurring fees, the recommendation would shift to no expansion or a different value proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. Test "Home Barista Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: social positioning condition (emphasizing the third-place coffee experience) or convenience positioning condition (emphasizing quick, easy brewing). They are then shown a product description of a compact, feature-rich espresso machine and asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.. Sample: 300 participants, recruited from a panel of home baristas and coffee enthusiasts, balanced across the two conditions.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (on a 7-point scale) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the social positioning condition compared to the convenience condition.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the convenience positioning condition compared to the social positioning condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP in the social positioning condition exceeds the average WTP in the convenience positioning condition by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, we conclude that social interaction drives demand and support T1. If the average WTP in the convenience positioning condition exceeds the average WTP in the social positioning condition by at least 1.5 points, we conclude that convenience drives demand and support T2. If the difference is within 1.5 points or both conditions show similar WTP, we conclude the evidence is inconclusive and the theories remain open.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Method: Online choice experiment with two product variants: (A) Premium health‑focused variant emphasizing superior taste and purity; (B) Sustainability‑focused variant emphasizing reduced plastic waste and environmental impact. Participants view each variant and indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not at all likely to 7‑extremely likely to purchase).. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark and Turkey (150 per segment) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent score for each variant and the difference in intent between the two variants.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent for the premium variant than for the sustainability variant.; T2: Higher purchase intent for the sustainability variant than for the premium variant.. Decision rule: If the premium variant’s average intent exceeds the sustainability variant’s intent by at least 1.5 points on the 7‑point scale, proceed with a premium‑priced differentiated proposition. If the sustainability variant’s intent exceeds the premium variant’s intent by at least 1.5 points, pursue a sustainability‑focused proposition. If the difference is below 1.5 points, no. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

Sample: 200 homeowners and 200 small businesses/housing providers, recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution.. Method: Run a 12‑week pilot in two distinct locations: a residential building (e.g., a multi‑family apartment complex) and a small gym or fitness center.
