Track the following metrics: (1) trial adoption rate (number of units used by residents or gym members within 12 weeks); (2) purchase intent measured via a short survey asking about willingness to pay a premium price (e.g., 20% above comparable consumer units); and (3) wholesale sales data (if the unit is sold through a distributor, track units sold).. Sample: Residential pilot: 50 units placed in 10 buildings, targeting 2,000 residents. Small business pilot: 20 units placed in 10 gyms, targeting 2,000 gym members.. Measure: Trial adoption rate (percentage of units used by residents or gym members within 12 weeks) and purchase intent (percentage of surveyed residents or gym owners indicating intent to purchase at a premium price).. Predictions: T1: Residential pilot adoption rate ≥ 10% and purchase intent ≥ 20% of surveyed residents; small business pilot adoption rate ≤ 10% and purchase intent ≤ 15% of surveyed gym owners.; T2: Small business pilot adoption rate ≥ 15% and purchase intent ≥ 20% of surveyed gym owners; residential pilot adoption rate ≤ 10% and purchase intent ≤ 15% of surveyed residents.. Decision rule: If the residential pilot meets both adoption threshold (10%) and purchase intent threshold (20%), proceed to develop a differentiated residential proposition. Test "Differentiated Purifier Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a premium‑priced purifier messaging emphasizing taste and purity; Group B sees a sustainability‑focused purifier messaging emphasizing reduced plastic waste. Both groups see a standard‑priced purifier as a baseline. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not at all likely to 7‑extremely likely) and state their top reason for choosing the product.. Sample: 400 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced across both groups (200 per group).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑to 7) and top reason for choosing the product.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group B, and taste and purity will be the top reason for Group A.; T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group A, and sustainability will be the top reason for Group B.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 5.5), proceed to develop a premium‑priced differentiated proposition targeting taste and purity. If Group B’s average is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A (i.e., Group B’s average ≥ 5.5), proceed to develop a sustainability‑focused differentiated proposition targeting eco‑friendly attributes. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and continue focusing on current B2B membranes.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium taste and purity, targeting health‑conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for superior water quality. Use the proposed messaging test to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated result SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer motivations related to taste, purity, or premium pricing. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium taste and purity, targeting health‑conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for superior water quality. Use the proposed messaging test to validate demand before scaling. Target customer: Health‑conscious consumers in Denmark who currently use standard water purifiers and are willing to pay a premium for perceived taste and purity.. Value proposition: A premium‑priced home water purifier that delivers superior taste and purity through Aquaporin’s biomimetic membranes, positioned as a lifestyle health product.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 6‑week online survey test with 400 Danish adults, comparing premium messaging (taste/purity) against sustainability messaging, and apply the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with a differentiated product.. Uncertainty: The size of the premium price premium consumers are willing to pay for taste and purity is unknown; the test will resolve this. Also, the sustainability message’s impact on purchase intent is uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the premium and sustainability messages, or if the sustainability message outperforms the premium message, we would reconsider the positioning and focus on eco‑friendly.; If the premium messaging fails to achieve the 1.5‑point threshold, we would abandon the differentiated proposition and continue focusing on B2B membranes.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Self-Service vs Compact Unit Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a self-service laundry unit description (highlighting convenience and time savings) or a compact, professional‑grade unit description (highlighting small‑footprint and labor‑cost savings). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑Very unlikely to 7‑Very likely).. Sample: 300 adult consumers (150 per arm) recruited via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑90) for each unit description.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent for the self‑service unit (average ≥ 5.5) than for the compact unit.; T2: Higher purchase intent for the compact unit (average ≥ 5.5) than for the self‑service unit.. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and focus on existing professional offerings.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

T1: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that simplifies meal preparation, because they value convenience and recurring revenue. Who benefits: Home cooks seeking time-saving cooking solutions and subscription services.. Why behaviour changes: A subscription model reduces upfront cost and provides ongoing updates, making the product more attractive than a one-time purchase.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can capture value through recurring subscription fees and premium pricing for smart features, while also leveraging its existing B2B relationships to reach consumers.. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a subscription fee for convenience.; The smart features are perceived as valuable enough to justify the subscription cost.; RATIONAL can integrate a subscription platform into its existing product line without significant additional development.. Predictions: In a test offering a subscription-based combi-steamer, at least 30% of respondents will sign up within 6 weeks.; Surveyed home cooks will report a willingness to pay a monthly fee of €20-€30 for the device.; Adoption rates will be higher among younger, tech-savvy consumers compared to older demographics..

T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is positioned as a premium, high-performance appliance that signals professional quality and status, because they view cooking as a lifestyle and are willing to pay for brand prestige. Who benefits: Home cooks who value brand prestige, professional-grade performance, and status signaling.. Why behaviour changes: A premium positioning creates a perception of higher quality and exclusivity, leading consumers to choose the product over cheaper alternatives.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can capture value through premium pricing, limited-edition designs, and brand marketing that emphasizes professional heritage, while also leveraging its existing B2B reputation to attract home consumers.. Assumptions: Home cooks are price-sensitive and prioritize brand perception over cost.; Professional-grade performance is a key purchase driver for home cooks.; RATIONAL can effectively communicate its professional heritage to home consumers without diluting its commercial image.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced combi-steamer, at least 25% of respondents will choose it over a lower-priced alternative.; Surveyed home cooks will report willingness to pay at least 20% more for a product marketed as "professional-grade" compared to a standard model.; Adoption rates will be higher among consumers who already own professional-grade kitchen equipment..

Test "Subscription vs Premium Positioning Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 German adults (250 per arm) recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Measure: 1) WTP: maximum monthly fee (EUR) a respondent would pay for the device. 2) Choice: percentage selecting "Subscription" vs "Premium" option. 3) Intent to purchase: binary (would buy).. Predictions: T1: Subscription arm shows higher WTP and higher "Subscription" choice than Premium arm; Premium arm shows low intent.; T2: Premium arm shows higher WTP and higher "Premium" choice than Subscription arm; Subscription arm shows low intent.. Decision rule: If Subscription arm WTP ≥ €30 and Premium arm WTP < €20, recommend Subscription positioning (T1). Else if Premium arm WTP ≥ €30 and Subscription arm WTP < €20, recommend Premium positioning (T2). If neither condition is met, inconclusive and no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

case.question: Should RATIONAL develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks, building on its commercial combi-steamer technology, or stay with professional kitchens? What evidence would justify either choice?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Who benefits: Home cooks gain time and reduced effort; RATIONAL benefits from recurring subscription revenue and premium pricing.. Why behaviour changes: Smart home integration and subscription model reduce upfront cost and provide ongoing value, making the appliance attractive for occasional use.. How value is captured: RATIONAL captures value through subscription fees and premium pricing for smart features, while also leveraging its existing B2B reputation.. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay recurring fees for smart cooking features.; Smart home integration is accessible and affordable for residential users.; Subscription model can be scaled without cannibalizing professional sales.. Predictions: In a test offering a smart, subscription-based combi-steamer, at least 30% of surveyed home cooks will sign up for the subscription within 12 weeks.; Willingness to pay for the subscription will be at least 20% of the device's price, indicating price sensitivity..

T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is positioned as a premium, high-performance appliance that emphasizes professional-grade cooking performance, because they seek superior results and are willing to pay for advanced technology. Who benefits: Home cooks gain professional-quality cooking results; RATIONAL benefits from premium pricing and brand differentiation.. Why behaviour changes: Demand for high performance and brand prestige drives home cooks to choose appliances that deliver superior results, even at higher price points.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium, high-performance combi-steamer, at least 25% of surveyed home cooks will express intent to purchase at a price 20% above the standard model.; Surveyed home cooks will rank performance and brand prestige higher than price when evaluating the appliance..

Test "Smart vs Premium Subscription Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two parallel arms: Arm A offers a smart, subscription-based combi-steamer at a fixed price; Arm B offers a premium, high-performance combi-steamer at a fixed price. Participants are randomly assigned to one arm. Both arms include a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question and a purchase intent question.. Sample: 500 adult home cooks (aged 25-55) recruited via an online panel, balanced across both arms.. Measure: 1) Percentage of participants who indicate they would purchase the device at the given price. 2) Average WTP (in euros) for each arm. 3) Purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Predictions: T1: Arm A will show at least 30% purchase intent and an average WTP at least 20% of the device price, indicating demand for a subscription-based model. Arm B will show lower purchase intent and lower WTP.; T2: Arm B will show at least 25% purchase intent and an average WTP at least 20% of the device price, indicating demand for a premium, high-performance model. Arm A will show lower purchase intent and lower WTP.. Decision rule: If Arm A’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its average WTP is at least 20% of the device price, proceed with a subscription-based home‑cook proposition. If Arm B’s purchase intent is at least 25% and its average WTP is at least 20% of the device price, proceed with a premium, high‑performance home‑cook proposition. If neither arm meets its threshold, do not expand into either segment.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing B2B reputation and smart home integration capabilities. The test should validate willingness to pay for recurring subscription fees and purchase intent at a price 20% above the standard model. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cook demand for a subscription-based combi-steamer or their willingness to pay recurring fees. It tests coordination friction, not subscription willingness to pay, so it does not affect T1. New claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, recurring revenue device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and ongoing value.. Evidence: SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing B2B reputation and smart home integration capabilities. The test should validate willingness to pay for recurring subscription fees and purchase intent at a price 20% above the standard model. Target customer: Home cooks (aged 25‑55) who value convenience, recurring value, and are open to smart home integration.. Value proposition: A subscription‑based combi-steamer that automates cooking, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing value, reducing upfront cost and offering recurring revenue for RATIONAL.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Smart vs Premium Subscription Test (500 participants, 6 weeks, €8,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the subscription model.. Uncertainty: The test will determine whether home cooks are willing to pay recurring subscription fees and whether the subscription model can be scaled without cannibalizing professional sales. The source does not provide evidence of demand for a smart,. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 30% or average willingness to pay below 20% of the device price, the recommendation would shift to a premium, high‑performance model.; If additional evidence shows strong demand for smart home integration and recurring revenue, the recommendation would be to prioritize a subscription‑based model.; If the test confirms strong brand prestige and performance as primary drivers, the recommendation would be to emphasize premium positioning.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.; Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.; Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).; 2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.; 4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).; 5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition..

T1: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions because they value convenience and cost savings, and are willing to pay a premium for a self‑service option that reduces wait times and labor costs. Who benefits: Homeowners and small businesses seeking affordable, hands‑free laundry solutions.. Why behaviour changes: Growing demand for convenience and desire to lower monthly laundry expenses drive homeowners to choose self‑service machines over traditional laundromats.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by selling premium‑priced consumer‑oriented machines through retail channels, leveraging its professional‑grade reliability and brand reputation.. Assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a price premium for convenience.; Self‑service adoption rates are higher in residential settings than in professional settings.; Retail distribution can reach target consumers effectively.. Predictions: In a test market, consumers will choose a self‑service machine over a laundromat at a higher rate.; Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% above the cost of a standard professional machine.; Sales conversion in a pilot retail store will exceed a baseline of 5 units per week..

T2: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions because they value resource efficiency and environmental sustainability, and are willing to pay a premium for machines that reduce water and energy consumption. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious homeowners and small businesses seeking sustainable laundry solutions.. Why behaviour changes: Growing awareness of water and energy waste in traditional laundromats drives homeowners to choose machines that offer lower operational costs and a smaller environmental footprint.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by positioning its consumer machines as eco‑friendly, offering premium pricing and potentially receiving incentives for energy‑efficient products.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a price premium for eco‑friendly products.; Energy‑efficient machines offer measurable cost savings compared to conventional models.; Regulatory or market pressures will continue to favor sustainable appliances.. Predictions: In a test market, eco‑friendly machines will achieve higher purchase intent among environmentally conscious consumers.; Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% above the cost of a standard professional machine.; Sales conversion in a pilot eco‑focused retail store will exceed a baseline of 4 units per week..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Eco‑Friendliness" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with simulated purchase decisions.. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners (recruited via panel) who have experienced laundry challenges (e.g., long wait times, high utility bills).. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay premium (percentage willing to pay at least 20% above a standard professional machine price). 2) Choice frequency (percentage selecting self‑service over laundromat).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will choose the self‑service machine at a higher rate and show higher willingness to pay a premium than eco‑friendly machines.; T2: Homeowners will choose the eco‑friendly machine at a higher rate and show higher willingness to pay a premium than convenience‑focused machines.. Decision rule: If the self‑service machine achieves a choice rate ≥ 40% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 20% among homeowners, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the eco‑friendly machine achieves a choice rate ≥ 40% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 20%, develop an eco‑friendly proposition. If neither meets both thresholds, do not expand into consumer markets.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and small businesses, emphasizing convenience and cost savings through self-service laundry solutions. Begin with a limited pilot in retail channels to test demand and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for self-service laundry solutions. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and small businesses, emphasizing convenience and cost savings through self-service laundry solutions. Begin with a limited pilot in retail channels to test demand and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and small businesses seeking affordable, hands‑free laundry solutions.. Value proposition: Premium‑priced self‑service machines that reduce wait times, labor costs, and monthly utility expenses, leveraging Electron’x Professional’s professional‑grade reliability and brand reputation.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to validate choice rates and willingness to pay premiums for self‑service versus eco‑friendly machines.. Uncertainty: The willingness to pay premium for convenience and the relative demand for eco‑friendly features are uncertain. Evidence from the Consumer Preference Test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the test shows the eco‑friendly machine achieving a choice rate ≥ 40% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 20%, we would shift focus to an eco‑friendly consumer proposition.; If neither self‑service nor eco‑friendly machines meet both thresholds, we would recommend no expansion into consumer markets.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Convenience vs. Status Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from home cooks (self-identified) and professional kitchen users. Each participant views a product description of a RATIONAL combi-steamer and is asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). Messaging is randomized between a convenience framing (time-saving, cleanup reduction) and a status framing (professional‑grade, premium).. Sample: 500 participants: 250 home cooks (self‑identified) and 250 professional kitchen users. Recruit via panel to ensure demographic balance.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and average willingness to pay (EUR) for each frame.. Test "Home Cook Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized product exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 home cooks recruited via a panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: "Would you buy this differentiated combi-steamer at a premium price?" (binary: Yes/No). 2) WTP premium: "How much more would you pay for this compared to a standard model?" (EUR). 3) Subscription preference: "Would you subscribe to a monthly recipe/service for this combi-steamer?" (binary: Yes/No).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher WTP premium for the differentiated premium model than for a standard model.; T2: Higher subscription preference and higher WTP for the subscription-based model than for the product-only model.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for the differentiated premium model exceeds 40% and its WTP premium exceeds 20% of the standard model's price, proceed with a differentiated premium home-cook proposition. If subscription preference exceeds 40% and WTP for the subscription model exceeds 20% of the premium model's price, pursue a subscription model. If neither condition is met, stay with professional kitchens.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated premium home-cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription-based combi-steamer) targeting frequent home cooks who value professional-grade convenience and quality. Target customer: Home cooks who cook frequently and want efficient, high-quality cooking solutions, particularly those who currently use multiple cooking devices.. Value proposition: A premium, professional-grade combi-steamer that combines steaming, boiling, and other functions in a single appliance, offering convenience, consistent results, and potential for recurring revenue through accessories or subscription.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Home Cook Preference Test (500 respondents, 8 weeks, €18,000) to validate purchase intent and willingness-to-pay for a differentiated premium model versus a standard model.. Uncertainty: The size of the home-cook market, willingness to pay a premium, and the effectiveness of a subscription model remain uncertain. The test will clarify these points before committing resources.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 40% or WTP premium below 20% of the standard model's price, we would abandon the premium home-cook proposition and stay focused on professional kitchens.; If the test demonstrates strong subscription preference and WTP for a subscription model, we would pursue a subscription-based model.; If new evidence shows home cooks prefer entry-level appliances over premium professional-grade devices, we would reconsider the premium positioning.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

case.question: Should RATIONAL develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks, building on its commercial combi-steamer technology, or stay with professional kitchens? What evidence would justify either choice?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. Test "Smart vs Premium Combi-Steamer Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase decision.. Sample: 500 adult home cooks recruited via panel, balanced for gender and cooking frequency ( weekly vs monthly).. Measure: 1) Willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each feature (smart automation, subscription, premium performance). 2) Purchase intent (would buy now vs would not buy). 3) Actual purchase intent (if offered a discount).. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP for smart automation and subscription than for premium performance; purchase intent for smart package exceeds premium package.; T2: Higher WTP for premium performance and durability than for smart automation; purchase intent for premium package exceeds smart package.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for smart automation exceeds premium performance by at least 10% and purchase intent for smart package exceeds premium package by at least 15%, recommend developing a differentiated home-cook proposition focused on smart automation and subscription (support T1). If premium performance exceeds smart automation by at least 10% and purchase intent for premium package exceeds smart package by at least 15%, recommend a premium positioning proposition (support T2). If neither difference meets its threshold, recommend no expansion (status quo).. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..

case.question: Should Simonelli Group develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing professional espresso-equipment offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: The Eagle One Prima is Victoria Arduino’s flagship espresso machine for the domestic market. The name “prima” comes from being the Italian manufacturer’s “first step towards a new frontier” and first machine in a long time catered to coffee at home.
You’re forgetting the one thing being a home barista can never offer: social interaction! The cafe is a true third place in many peoples’ lives, and everyone is starved for that!

Italian espresso machine company La Marzocco has unveiled the Linea Micra, a compact dual-boiler espresso machine designed squarely for home use. The approximately $3,900 machine (United States market) represents the smallest and least expensive machine in the growing La Marzocco Home espresso machine line.

At the same time, the professional division maintained excellent momentum throughout the year, achieving revenue growth of over 40% in the fourth quarter. Both brands, La Marzocco and Eversys, delivered outstanding results, driven by the consolidated leadership of our products in the premium segments, the ability to intercept emerging trends in specialty coffee, and the rapid expansion into the prosumer market.

In terms of product segments, the difficult comparison with the extraordinary performance of the quarters of the previous two years led to a decline for all of the macro categories of the "consumer" business, including coffee as well.

Comparing the composition in 2024 with 2023, the situation is steady, with the largest decreases of shares recorded for housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels, followed by furnishings, household equipment and routine household maintenance (both -0.2 pp). By contrast, the largest increases in shares between 2023 and 2024 were recorded for restaurants and accommodation services (+0.2 pp) followed by recreation, sport and culture and health (both +0.1 pp).

While there is evidence to suggest that consumer knowledge and the prosumer market have grown significantly, it’s unlikely that we will see sustained demand for high-end coffee equipment. After an initial surge during the pandemic, there are signs that coffee equipment sales have since slowed.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.; Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.; Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.; 2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.; 3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.; 4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments..

T1: Home barista consumers will adopt a differentiated Simonelli consumer product if they perceive it as a premium, easy-to-use machine for personal coffee preparation, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay. Who benefits: Simonelli Group gains higher margin sales and brand extension into consumer markets.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from professional equipment to home use when they view the product as convenient and stylish, reducing perceived complexity and increasing leisure value.. How value is captured: Simonelli can command premium pricing for design, materials, and brand positioning, and potentially cross-sell accessories or subscription services.. Assumptions: Home barista market is large enough to support a differentiated entry point.; Simonelli has the design and manufacturing capacity to create a consumer-friendly product.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product they perceive as easy to use and stylish.. Predictions: A test offering a compact, entry-level home barista machine will generate higher purchase intent than a standard professional machine.; Willingness to pay for the home machine will be at least 20% above the price of a comparable professional model.; Surveyed home barista participants will cite ease of use and design as primary purchase drivers..

T2: Simonelli will not expand into consumer markets because the overall consumer coffee market is declining, and the company is focused on its professional and commercial segments, limiting its ability to capture consumer demand. Who benefits: Simonelli Group benefits from maintaining its current revenue base and avoiding resource allocation to a potentially unprofitable consumer segment.. Why behaviour changes: The decline in consumer coffee sales and the company’s strategic focus on professional and commercial segments make it unlikely that Simonelli will invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. How value is captured: Simonelli can sustain its current profitability by not diverting resources to a consumer market that is not expected to grow.. Assumptions: The consumer coffee market is in decline, as evidenced by the 2023 Q1 results showing a decline across all consumer product segments.; Simonelli’s current revenue is primarily from professional and commercial segments, limiting its ability to compete in consumer markets.; The company has no existing consumer products or distribution channels to leverage.. Predictions: A test offering a consumer product will show low purchase intent or sales, indicating that the market is not large enough to justify investment.; Simonelli’s revenue from consumer segments will remain low or negative, supporting the assumption that the market is declining.; Consumers will not express willingness to pay a premium for a Simonelli consumer product, contradicting the assumption that consumers are willing to pay for a differentiated offering..

Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a product description of a compact, entry-level home barista machine (Simonelli) and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2‑ very unlikely to 7‑2‑ very likely). They are also asked about maximum willingness to pay and a brief qualitative reason.. Sample: 300 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age to reflect home barista demographics. Recruitment target: self-identified home baristas or coffee enthusiasts aged 25–45.. Measure: 1) Average purchase intent score (mean of 7-point scale). 2) Maximum willingness to pay (highest stated price). 3) Qualitative reason for purchase intent (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Average purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and willingness to pay ≥ €1,200, with ease of use and design cited as primary drivers.; T2: Average purchase intent ≤ 4.5 and willingness to pay ≤ €1,000, with respondents citing market decline or lack of perceived need as reasons.. Decision rule: If average purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and willingness to pay ≥ €1,200, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If average purchase intent ≤ 4.5 and willingness to pay ≤ €1,000, do not invest in a consumer expansion. If intent is between 4.5 and 5.5 and willingness to pay is between €1,000 and €1,200, conduct a smaller test of willingness to pay and design.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

T1: Home barista demand is driven by lifestyle and social sharing, making a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., a premium machine with design and connectivity) attractive to individual buyers who want to showcase their coffee experience. Who benefits: Simonelli Group would capture value by selling premium pricing to consumers who view the machine as a status symbol and share their coffee journey on social media.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers increasingly adopt coffee equipment as part of their lifestyle and social identity, seeking products that reflect their personal style and can be proudly displayed.. How value is captured: Simonelli can charge higher prices for a differentiated product and sell through premium channels like online retail and specialty coffee shops, leveraging the home barista trend.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a machine that looks and functions as a lifestyle item.; Social sharing of coffee experiences drives purchase decisions among home baristas.; Simonelli can effectively market and distribute a differentiated consumer product within budget.. Predictions: If a test offers a design-forward, social-sharing-friendly machine at a premium price, individual buyers will express higher intent to purchase compared to a standard professional model.; Sales of the differentiated product will be concentrated among consumers who frequently post about coffee on social media..

T2: Home barista demand is driven by convenience and time-saving features, making a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., compact, easy-to-use machine) attractive to busy individuals who need quick, high-quality coffee. Who benefits: Simonelli Group would capture value by offering a product that simplifies coffee preparation, allowing consumers to spend less time and more time on other activities.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers with limited time seek equipment that reduces the effort of making coffee, leading them to prefer machines that are easy to operate and compact.. How value is captured: Simonelli can price the product at a premium for its convenience features and sell through retail channels that cater to busy consumers, such as supermarkets and online marketplaces.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience over design or status when choosing coffee equipment.; A compact, easy-to-use machine reduces the perceived effort of coffee preparation.; Simonelli can produce and market a convenient consumer product within budget.. Predictions: If a test offers a compact, easy-to-use machine, consumers will report higher satisfaction with coffee preparation time compared to a standard professional model.; Sales of the differentiated product will be concentrated among consumers who frequently juggle multiple tasks and need quick coffee solutions..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Lifestyle vs. Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a design-forward, premium-priced home barista machine with social-sharing features (e.g., Instagram-friendly design, connectivity). Group B sees a compact, easy-to-use machine with time-saving features (e.g., quick brewing, compact size). Both groups are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the top reason for choosing the product.. Sample: 300 adult consumers interested in coffee, recruited via an online panel. 150 per group to ensure statistical power.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary reason for choosing the product (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and will cite social sharing as the primary reason.; T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and will cite convenience as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 5.5), conclude that lifestyle/social-sharing motivation drives demand and T1 is more likely. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, conclude convenience drives demand and T2 is more likely. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Test "Subscription vs Premium Messaging Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a subscription-based combi-steamer description emphasizing automation, recurring revenue, and recipe access. Group B receives a premium-priced combi-steamer description emphasizing precision cooking, professional-grade results, and high performance. Both groups see the same product specifications and price point.. Sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay a recurring subscription fee (EUR 9.99/month).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay the subscription fee than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay the premium price than Group A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A average >= 5.5), proceed with the subscription-based differentiated proposition. If the average purchase intent for Group B is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A (i.e., Group B average >= 5.5), proceed with the premium-priced differentiated proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not expand into either segment.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.
